name: Poppy Underbough
equipment: A small map of the Shamble drawn on cured rat-skin (surprisingly accurate)
A carved wooden token in the shape of a crow (meaning unknown)
A spool of fine silk rope (50 feet)
A collection of copper coins from six different noble houses (a record of who she has picked pockets from)
features: Lucky (Lightfoot Halfling racial — when you roll a 1 on the d20 for an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw, you can reroll the die; you must use the new roll, which is enormously valuable and fires more often than players expect)
Brave (Halfling racial — you have advantage on saving throws against being frightened; you may still be scared, but fear does not control you)
Halfling Nimbleness (Halfling racial — you can move through the space of any creature that is of a size larger than yours; useful for slipping past guards and through crowds)

Naturally Stealthy (Lightfoot Halfling racial — you can attempt to hide even when you are obscured only by a creature that is at least one size larger than you; you can vanish behind an ally mid-combat)

Expertise (Rogue level 1 — choose two skills or one skill and Thieves' Tools; you gain double your proficiency bonus on those checks; Poppy has Expertise in Stealth and Thieves' Tools, giving +7 to each at level 1)

Sneak Attack (Rogue level 1 — once per turn, you can deal an extra 1d6 damage to one creature you hit with an attack if you have advantage on the roll or if another enemy of the target is within 5 feet of it and you are not incapacitated; at level 1 this is 1d6 extra damage)

Thieves' Cant (Rogue level 1 — you know Thieves' Cant, a secret mixture of dialect, jargon, and code that allows you to hide messages in seemingly normal conversation; only another creature that knows Thieves' Cant understands such messages; it takes four times longer than usual to convey a message this way)

City Secrets (Urchin background — you know the secret patterns and flows of cities and can find passages through the urban sprawl that others would miss; when not in combat you can travel between any two locations in the city twice as fast as your speed would normally allow)

personality.traits: I talk too fast when I am excited, which is most of the time, and I have a habit of finishing other people's sentences when I already know what they mean to say — usually correctly, which makes it worse. I am constitutionally incapable of walking past a locked door without wondering what is behind it, which has gotten me into trouble approximately thirty-seven times and out of trouble twice.
personality.ideals: The city belongs to everyone who lives in it, not just the people who can afford to live on the high side of it. I take from people who have too much and I do not feel guilty about that. I feel guilty about other things, occasionally, but not about that.
personality.bonds: There is a woman in the Shamble named Marta who runs a bread stall and who fed me every morning for three years without ever asking anything in return. She does not know it, but I have been keeping the Gutter Wolves off her street for two years by ensuring their leadership has regular, unexplained bad luck with their coin purses. I would do a great deal to keep Marta safe.
personality.flaws: I am constitutionally suspicious of authority and have a terrible habit of stealing small things I do not need from people I like, apparently to reassure myself that they cannot control me. I am aware this is a problem. I have not solved it.

appearance: Poppy Underbough stands three feet and a few stubborn inches tall, which is about right for a Lightfoot halfling of twenty-two years and is absolutely the last thing an adversary is supposed to think about before Poppy's dagger finds their kidney. She is slight and quick-boned, with the coiled, efficient movement of a rat in a familiar building — someone who knows where every beam and crack is and uses that knowledge constantly. Her hair is a dark chestnut tangle cut close on the sides and left deliberately messy on top, and her eyes are a warm, intelligent hazel that shift toward amber in firelight. Her face is round and mobile, expressive in the way of someone who learned early that a good expression can close a door before someone decides to look behind it — an easy grin, a baffled brow, a sincere-looking pair of wide eyes deployed with professional precision. Her skin is olive-brown and covered on the arms and neck with a collection of small scars, the kind accumulated over years of moving through places with sharp edges and owners who object to being entered. She dresses in layers of brown and charcoal grey that have been carefully dirtied to the exact shade of the Shamble's walls, wears soft-soled shoes of her own cobbling, and carries her two daggers in sheaths sewn into the lining of her jacket rather than on open belt loops. The silk rope is coiled around her waist under her jacket like a broad belt. The rat-skin map is tucked into her left boot.
backstory:
Poppy Underbough does not know her family name. Underbough is what the children in the Shamble called her when she was very small, because she slept under a particular half-collapsed staircase near the river and was always emerging from it, and names given to children by other children in the Shamble tend to stick the way mud sticks to boots: thoroughly and without permission.

Her earliest memories are of the Thieves' Market — not the permanent stalls of the outer ring, but the temporary pitches of the inner alleys that appear at dusk and disappear by dawn, where the merchandise is anything the day's work brought in and the price is whatever the seller can argue for. She was running small packages for market traders by the time she was six, picking pockets by eight, and doing second-story entry work for the Carmine Veil's Shamble sub-agents by twelve. She was never formally recruited into the Veil — she is too independent, too chaotic for their structures, and she made the strategic decision very early that staying outside an organization you work adjacent to gives you options that membership forecloses.

Coronne's rooftops are Poppy's native environment in a way the streets are not. At street level she is one more small person in a crowd, easy to overlook and easy to underestimate; above the eaves, on the flat tile expanses of the high Shamble tenements and the wider lead-flashed roofs of the counting houses near the market, she is genuinely extraordinary. She knows three routes between any two points in the city that use nothing lower than a second-story gutter, and on a still night she can cover the distance from the Drowned Cat to the Thieves' Market in under ten minutes without touching the ground. She uses this knowledge practically and constantly. She has never considered it remarkable.

The carved wooden crow token in her pack came from the first person she ever stole from who, when they caught her red-handed, chose to laugh instead of hitting her. An old forger named Sable, who worked out of a narrow print-shop near the river, told Poppy she had good hands and offered her a cup of something hot and the token — which, Sable said, was from a game whose rules Poppy would understand when she was ready. Sable died of winter fever two years later and never explained the game. Poppy has kept the token and thought about it often.

She was in the Shamble the night the Old Quarter burned, as she always is when something interesting happens at midnight, and she saw the man with the ledger before the others did. She saw the Veil dagger, too, and recognized the style of it, and understood in one cold, clear moment that the ledger was either the most valuable or the most dangerous thing in the Shamble that night, and probably both. She also understood that the men coming back for it would not want witnesses. Being constitutionally opposed to being murdered and genuinely incapable of ignoring something this interesting, she did what Poppy Underbough has always done when the choice is between discretion and curiosity: she went toward it.
